title: Case study: reproduction number and mobility in China
text: case study reproduces reproduction-number/mobility analysis Ainslie et al. (2020) [1], examined whether China’s COVID-19 outbreak remained control social distancing policies relaxed early 2020, using relationship estimated effective reproduction number (Rt, average number new cases generated single case) population mobility one line evidence. pika originally developed support analysis: estimating Rt region, determining lag mobility Rt strongly correlated, tracking correlation evolves time via rolling window. Reproducing paper’s key numbers useful check package : following steps bundled data recovers paper’s headline finding four-day lag mobility Rt Hubei province, subsequent pattern correlation weakening reversing sign movement resumed – rather just workflow superficially resembles paper’s. vignette walks workflow – estimate_rt() -> cross_corr() -> rolling_corr() -> plot_corr() – china_case_data exante_movement_data example datasets bundled package. See vignette("wastewater-surveillance") lag-detection rolling-correlation workflow applied different domain.

title: Case study: reproduction number and mobility in China
text: estimate effective reproduction number (Rt), pika function estimate_rt() provides wrapper EpiEstim::estimate_R() [4] enables users estimate Rt grouping variable. input estimate_rt() takes data frame daily cases deaths group. pika includes example data set china_case_data.rda includes daily reported cases COVID-19 several provinces China 16 January 2020 24 March 2020. estimate Rt case data, user must specify data set dat = argument estimate_rt(). data set include three columns: date column (class ‘date’), grouping variable, value used estimate Rt (commonly cases, quantities can used, deaths). names columns input data set specified character strings grp_var =, date_var =, incidence_var = arguments. method used estimate Rt can changed using est_method = argument. argument takes following options: c("non_parametric_si","parametric_si","uncertain_si","si_from_data","si_from_sample"). methods require specifying mean standard deviation serial interval, parameters can set using si_mean = si_std = function arguments. default values si_mean = 6.48 si_std = 3.83 [5]. information methodology underlying EpiEstim::estimate_R look vignette help("estimate_R").
code: # to estimate them with pika, use estimate_rt() ------------------------------------------ rt_estimates <- estimate_rt(dat = china_case_data,                             grp_var = "province",                             date_var = "date",                             incidence_var = "cases"                             ) %>%   # a little data formatting--------------------------------------------------------------   mutate(province = to_snake_case(province)) %>%   select(-date_start) %>%   rename("date" = "date_end")

title: Case study: reproduction number and mobility in China
text: determining relationship two time series sometimes interest determine lag correlation two time series highest, ’ll call optimal lag. determine optimal lag, two time series must first merged single data frame. using dplyr’s left_join() date province. can identify optimal lag calculating cross correlation two time series grouping variable different lags using cross_corr function. argument max_lag = specifies maximum lag test. example set 10 days. subset_date = argument allows user determine cross correlation two time series subset time window; original paper, focus period 15 February 2020, peak outbreak Hubei province. expect changes movement precede changes Rt, since takes time change contact patterns show transmission case reports, movement x_var Rt y_var (cross_corr() restricts lags zero negative, .e. x_var ahead y_var). recovers four-day lag Hubei – matching four-day lag reported Ainslie et al. (2020) giving highest correlation movement Rt – lags zero one day regions, also consistent paper’s region-specific sensitivity analysis. Following paper, “backdate” Rt estimates lag (.e. shift region’s Rt dates earlier lag days, negative number zero, lag zero leaves dates unchanged), without altering dates movement data, Rt value lines movement value strongly associated .
code: # Join data sets together by date and province to determine cross correlation ----------- # for this we are using input rt estimates, not those estimated using pika::estimate_rt() data_joined <- left_join(rt_estimates,                          exante_movement_data,                          by = c("date","province")                          ) # # Determine lag with max cross correlation between movement and Rt ---------------------- lags <- cross_corr(dat = data_joined,                    date_var = "date",                    grp_var = "province",                    x_var = "movement",                    y_var = "r_mean",                    max_lag = 10,                    subset_date = "2020-02-15"                   ) lags # backdate Rt estimates using the lag from cross_corr() ---------------------------------- data_joined_lag <- rt_estimates %>%   left_join(lags, by = "province") %>%   mutate(date = date + lag) %>%   select(-lag) %>%   left_join(exante_movement_data, by = c("date", "province"))

text: often interest determine relationship two time series, specifically rolling correlation. rolling_corr() function calculates rolling correlation two times series (x_var y_var) specified time window n =. , calculate biweekly rolling correlation Rt movement. Since data daily estimates Rt movement, set n = 14. data monthly wanted determine 6 month rolling correlation, set n = 6. output rolling_corr() data frame additional column added input dataset called “rolling_corr”. Depending value n, first n values “rolling_corr” NA. visualise rolling correlation, results rolling_corr() can plotted using plot_corr(). creates plot two time series rolling correlation facetted grouping variable. optional arguments change facet labels (facet_lables =), legend_labels (legend_labels =), add confidence bounds primary time series (x_var_lower = x_var_upper =), set maximum value y-axis (y_max =). code plots mean Rt estimates 95% confidence bands, movement index, biweekly correlation . also specify custom facet legend labels restrict y-axis maximum value 10.  Hubei, rolling correlation strongly positive (close 1) lockdown period February, declines turns strongly negative mid-March movement resumed – qualitative pattern described Ainslie et al. (2020): tight coupling mobility transmission restrictions force, breaking mobility recovered transmission remained suppressed.
code: # Determine rolling correlation between Rt and movement --------------------------------- data_corr <- rolling_corr(dat = data_joined_lag,                           date_var = "date",                           grp_var = "province",                           x_var = "r_mean",                           y_var = "movement",                           n = 14) # Plot Rt, movement, and correlation ---------------------------------------------------- my_labels <- c("beijing" = "Beijing", "guangdong" = "Guangdong", "henan" = "Henan",                "hong_kong_sar" = "Hong Kong SAR", "hubei" = "Hubei", "hunan" = "Hunan",                "zhejiang" = "Zhejiang") my_legend = c("Correlation", "Reproduction Number", "Movement")  plot_corr(dat = data_corr,           date_var = "date",           grp_var = "province",           x_var = "r_mean",           y_var = "movement",           x_var_lower = "r_q2.5",           x_var_upper = "r_q97.5",           facet_labels = my_labels,           legend_labels = my_legend,           y_max = 10           )

text: pika bundles weekly SARS-CoV-2 wastewater concentration COVID-19 case counts three US states (wastewater_data covid_case_data). Joining gives pair time series per state. cross_corr() finds lag (rows data – , weeks) two variables strongly correlated, separately level grp_var:  rolling_corr() calculates correlation two variables moving window, can see whether relationship stable time rather assuming single lag/correlation applies throughout: plot_corr() visualizes series alongside rolling correlation, faceted group:  plot_lag() plots histogram lags returned cross_corr() across groups, useful many groups three shown :
code: library(dplyr) library(pika)  data(wastewater_data) data(covid_case_data)  dat <- inner_join(wastewater_data, covid_case_data, by = c("state", "date")) %>%   mutate(log_conc = log(conc), log_cases = log(cases + 1)) lags <- cross_corr(   dat = dat, date_var = "date", grp_var = "state",   x_var = "log_conc", y_var = "log_cases", max_lag = 8 ) lags #> # A tibble: 3 × 2 #>   state        lag #>   <chr>      <dbl> #> 1 California    -1 #> 2 New York       0 #> 3 Ohio           0 dat_corr <- rolling_corr(   dat = dat, date_var = "date", grp_var = "state",   x_var = "log_conc", y_var = "log_cases", n = 12 ) tail(dat_corr, 3) #> # A tibble: 3 × 9 #>   state date           conc n_sites n_samples cases log_conc log_cases roll_corr #>   <chr> <date>        <dbl>   <int>     <int> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl> #> 1 Ohio  2023-03-06   3.72e7      71       138  8332     17.4      9.03     0.907 #> 2 Ohio  2023-03-13   3.87e7      71       139  7586     17.5      8.93     0.942 #> 3 Ohio  2023-03-20   3.70e7      71       136  7016     17.4      8.86     0.906 plot_corr(   dat = dat_corr, date_var = "date", grp_var = "state",   x_var = "log_conc", y_var = "log_cases" ) plot_lag(dat = lags, lag_var = "lag")

title: Case study: wastewater surveillance as a leading indicator for COVID-19 cases
text: pika bundles two example datasets case study, covering California, New York, Ohio: wastewater_data: weekly, state-level SARS-CoV-2 concentration wastewater, built site-level sample records published CDC National Wastewater Surveillance System (NWSS) [3]. state-week value population-weighted mean flow- population-normalized concentration (copies per person per day) across sites reporting week. covid_case_data: weekly newly reported COVID-19 cases three states, built cumulative case counts published New York Times [4]. series run early 2020 27 March 2023, date NYT repository stopped updating – also case study look forward . wastewater_data covid_case_data number sites contributing state-week grew substantially NWSS expanded, single site California April 2020 well 100 sites per state 2022-2023:  Concentration spans several orders magnitude, work log scale throughout, similarly log-transform cases (adding 1 first, since state-weeks zero newly reported cases early pandemic):
code: library(dplyr) library(knitr) library(pika)  data(wastewater_data) data(covid_case_data) library(ggplot2) ggplot(wastewater_data, aes(x = date, y = n_sites, colour = state)) +   geom_line() +   labs(x = NULL, y = "number of sites reporting", colour = NULL) +   theme_minimal() data_joined <- inner_join(wastewater_data, covid_case_data, by = c("state", "date")) %>%   mutate(log_conc = log(conc), log_cases = log(cases + 1))

title: Case study: wastewater surveillance as a leading indicator for COVID-19 cases
text: cross_corr() searches lags (units rows input data – , weeks, since series already aggregated one row per state per week) returns, group, lag cross-correlation x_var y_var highest, restricted lags zero (.e. x_var ahead y_var). treat wastewater concentration x_var cases y_var, negative lag means wastewater leads cases.  Wastewater leads cases one two weeks California Ohio, roughly contemporaneous cases New York. sit toward shorter end , within, range reported elsewhere: Peccia et al. (2020) found wastewater led -day case reports 0-2 days led cases (later) reporting date 6-8 days New Haven, Connecticut, systematic review 133 reported wastewater-case correlations across many studies found lead times 2-24 days, correlation coefficients -0.38 0.99 [1,5] – lag estimates (state-level, log-log) correlation strengths find later fall within broad published range, even though specific catchments, populations, time periods differ ways make exact match unlikely. align two series optimal lag, shift state’s wastewater dates forward -lag weeks (.e. lag rows, converted days since data weekly). lag returned cross_corr() units rows input data, necessarily days weeks – always check spacing data converting. also means cross_corr() implicitly assumes every row evenly spaced time: California’s series missing one week early (period single site reporting), one pair consecutive rows 14 days apart rather 7. one gap roughly 150 weeks, effect estimated lag negligible, real assumption worth checking data trusting returned lag.
code: lags <- cross_corr(   dat     = data_joined,   date_var = "date",   grp_var  = "state",   x_var    = "log_conc",   y_var    = "log_cases",   max_lag  = 8 ) lags #> # A tibble: 3 × 2 #>   state        lag #>   <chr>      <dbl> #> 1 California    -1 #> 2 New York       0 #> 3 Ohio           0 data_lagged <- data_joined %>%   left_join(lags, by = "state") %>%   mutate(date = date - lag * 7) %>%   select(state, date, log_conc) %>%   inner_join(     data_joined %>% select(state, date, log_cases, cases),     by = c("state", "date")   ) %>%   arrange(state, date)

what: Did the relationship hold up as case-reporting quality declined?
title: Case study: wastewater surveillance as a leading indicator for COVID-19 cases
text: -home rapid testing became widely available US around January 2022, increasing share infections never reported public health authorities. eroded reliability case counts measure true infection burden, expect rolling correlation wastewater cases trend downward early 2022. Contrary expectation, rolling correlation show systematic decline March 2022 three states – anything, median correlation similar slightly higher later period. rolling correlation visibly noisy throughout whole series plot , occasional weeks weak negative correlation periods, likely reflecting genuine week--week volatility 12-week window (holiday reporting effects, changes sites reported week) rather sustained regime change. contradict published evidence case ascertainment declined – answering different question. Boehm et al. (2023) [2] directly studied three California wastewater treatment plants 1 May 2022 found genuine divergence: specific wastewater concentration corresponded significantly lower reported case incidence date (intercept power-law relationship two shifted; example, one plant fell 0.29 -0.66). Critically, reported slope relationship – two series move together – differ significantly two periods two three sites. consistent , contrary , find : reported cases can become systematically depressed absolute level relative true infections (ascertainment problem, Boehm et al. measured) remaining reasonably proportional, still-correlated signal relative week--week trends (rolling_corr() measures ). result state-level, lower-resolution echo , independent replication – tested intercept shift way . One general caveat applies whole analysis: wastewater concentration case counts smooth, wave-shaped epidemic curves, two series share similar wave shape show substantial correlation even without genuine leading-indicator relationship . Lagged rolling correlation reduce risk relative single contemporaneous correlation, eliminate – shared “big wave, smaller wave” shape can inflate correlation within 12-week window regardless true lead time. standard limitation correlation-based lag detection epidemic time series generally, something specific dataset. useful result precisely complicates tidy assumption: state level, aggregating across many counties sewersheds, reported case counts appear remained reasonably proportional – biased – signal underlying trends throughout study period, even absolute ascertainment almost certainly fell. Whether holds finer geographic resolution (individual sewersheds vs. county case counts) natural follow-question, one single overall lag/correlation estimate – rather rolling version used – hidden volatility entirely, might supported “relationship degraded” narrative opposite depending weeks happened dominate estimate.
code: data_corr %>%   filter(!is.na(roll_corr)) %>%   mutate(period = ifelse(date < as.Date("2022-03-01"), "pre-2022-03", "post-2022-03")) %>%   group_by(state, period) %>%   summarise(     mean_corr   = round(mean(roll_corr), 2),     median_corr = round(median(roll_corr), 2),     .groups = "drop"   ) %>%   arrange(state, period) %>%   kable()

title: Find the lag at which cross-correlation between two time series is maximised — cross_corr
text: Computes cross-correlation function (CCF) x_var y_var lags -max_lag 0 using ccf, returns lag highest CCF group. non-positive lags considered (.e. x_var leading y_var), reflecting assumption changes primary series precede changes secondary series.

title: Find the lag at which cross-correlation between two time series is maximised — cross_corr
code: cross_corr(   dat,   date_var = NULL,   grp_var,   x_var,   y_var,   max_lag = 20,   subset_date = NULL )

title: Find the lag at which cross-correlation between two time series is maximised — cross_corr
text: dat data frame containing two time series grouping column. date_var Character string giving name date column. Required subset_date non-NULL. supplied, rows sorted date_var within group CCF computed (required ccf assumes row order chronological). NULL, dat must already sorted chronologically within group. grp_var Character string giving name grouping column. CCF computed separately within group. x_var Character string giving name primary (leading) time series column. y_var Character string giving name secondary (lagged) time series column. max_lag Integer.
